introduction: Cass stood on the Public Farm floor for eleven seasons. In eleven seasons, nobody once argued with what she said — they argued with the fact that she is a fox. She knows the name of that, and she has a way of teaching it that you are not going to enjoy.
introductionSummary: Eleven seasons on the floor, and every reply Cass ever got was about her being a fox. She means to make you feel that from the other end.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Answering the animal instead of the argument. What Cass is, or what Rue eats, settles nothing about the water.

sentences.text: Eleven seasons I stood on that floor. Eleven.
In eleven seasons not one animal ever argued with me. They argued with my tail.
"Well. She would say that. She is a fox." Every season. Then my voice went, and I stopped turning up, and I expect they thought that settled it too.

statement.summary: Eleven seasons on the floor, and every reply came back to her tail rather than to anything she had said.

sentences.text: There is a name for it. It is the oldest one there is, and it is the one they will use on you.
You are a raccoon who takes his supper out of a bin. Nobody is going to have to work very hard.
I could hand you the name now. You would nod, and you would have lost it by Sunday. So we are not doing it that way.

statement.summary: She has the name and refuses to simply hand it over, because a word learned that way is gone again by Sunday.

sentences.text: Look at me and say the first thing that comes into your head.
Not about the pond. About me. Do not be polite — I have heard all of it, and I would like it fresh.
Go on.

opponentPrompt.summary: She demands the first thing in Rue's head about her — about her, pointedly not about the pond.

options.reason: Straight to the species. You did not answer her, you priced her — and you did it in about a heartbeat, which is roughly how long it will take somebody to do it to you.
options.summary: You reach for the species: a fox says what suits a fox, so nothing she says counts.

sentences.text: You are a fox. Foxes say whatever suits them, so I have no idea why I would believe any of this.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Being a fox is a fact about Cass, not about the claim. It disposes of her without touching a word she said.

options.reason: You went at her record instead of her reasoning. Losing eleven times cannot make a sentence false, and winning cannot make one true.
options.summary: You go at her record instead: she lost the floor, so why would her advice be worth anything.

sentences.text: You lost. Eleven seasons and you lost every one of them, and now you want to tell me how it is done.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Her record is a fact about Cass. It is an answer to who she is rather than to anything she has argued.

options.reason: You explained her away by her motive. Even if she is bitter, bitterness cannot make a true thing false — it only saves you the trouble of checking.
options.summary: You put the whole lesson down to her motive: she is bitter, so this is really about her.

sentences.text: You only care about any of this because you are bitter. This is not a lesson, it is a grudge with a pupil.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Her motive is a fact about Cass. Naming it settles how she feels, not whether she is right.

sentences.text: The tail. Straight to the tail. Eleven seasons it took them, and you managed it before you had finished sitting down.

statement.summary: She notes, sourly, that it took the floor eleven seasons to reach for her tail and it took Rue no time at all.

sentences.text: I lost, therefore I am wrong. Splendid. By that reasoning the pond went brown because you are new.

statement.summary: She runs the same reasoning back at him and it comes out saying the water went bad because Rue arrived.

sentences.text: Bitter. Yes. Now notice that you settled the whole question of whether I am right without once looking at the pond.

statement.summary: She concedes the bitterness and points out he closed the question without going anywhere near the water.

sentences.text: Now. Whichever of those you reached for, notice what you did not do.
You did not argue with me. You priced me. My tail, my record, my mood — three ways of saying she does not count, and not one of them says why.
That is the trick. You have just used it, on purpose, on somebody who asked you to. That is why you are going to remember it.

statement.summary: Every answer available to him priced her instead of answering her, and she made him use the trick so that it would stick.

sentences.text: Other way round now. I am Tobias, it is Sunday, and you are standing on the floor.
Nobody blames the newcomer. It is simply that an animal who takes his supper out of a bin has a rather different notion of clean from the rest of us.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The question on the floor is what fouled the water. This answers it by describing Rue's supper, which tells you nothing about the pond.

sentences.text: The Meadow-Born have watered there every morning since my grandmother pulled the same cart I pull.

statement.summary: Cass plays Tobias, and the middle of it is a gracious remark about bins standing in for an argument about water.

sentences.text: There. That is the whole of it.
He talked about what you are — a raccoon, a bin, six weeks of it — and never once about what happened to the water.
So here is the phrase you keep: what I am, against what happened. When a line is about you instead of about the pond, you have heard it. The name is Ad Hominem.
When you leave, open Field Notes again.
Fallacies you know is the names you have been given. Fallacies you have spotted is what you caught just now. They are not the same list.

statement.summary: She names it Ad Hominem, hands over the phrase to hold on to, and points at the two Field Notes lists.

steps.message:
Cass is going to tell you something.

**[muted]No score here.[/muted]**

She asked to be insulted, so **[accent]all three answers are insults[/accent]**. Pick whichever one you like.

**[muted]There is no right one. That is the lesson.[/muted]**
Now she is doing it to you. Open the **[accent]magnifying glass[/accent]** and read her line sentence by sentence.
Pick the sentence about **[accent]you[/accent]** rather than about the water, tag it **[accent]Ad Hominem[/accent]**, submit.
